extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning discrete mathematics (relations, closures, equivalence relations)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, existence theorems, examples, and basic properties for reflexive/symmetric/transitive closures, strict orders, and equivalence relations; includes proof strategies and exercises for students in a discrete math course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflexive closure (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation S ⊆ A×A is the reflexive closure of R if (1) R ⊆ S, (2) S is reflexive, and (3) for every relation T ⊆ A×A, if R ⊆ T and T is reflexive, then S ⊆ T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes the idea of 'adding just those ordered pairs required to make R reflexive.' If a reflexive closure exists it is unique (smallest element in the family of reflexive supersets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and construction of reflexive closure (Theorem 4.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every relation R on A has a reflexive closure; specifically S = R ∪ i_A (where i_A is the identity relation) is the reflexive closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: define S = R ∪ i_A and verify the three clauses of the reflexive-closure definition. Commentary emphasizes specifying the candidate S, then proving (1) R ⊆ S, (2) S is reflexive (i_A ⊆ S), and (3) S is smallest by letting T be an arbitrary reflexive superset and showing S ⊆ T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreflexive / strict partial order / strict total order (Definition 4.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: R is irreflexive if ∀x∈A ((x,x)∉R). R is a strict partial order if it is irreflexive and transitive. R is a strict total order if it is a strict partial order and satisfies trichotomy: ∀x∀y (xRy ∨ yRx ∨ x = y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: 'strict partial order' is not a partial order (it's not reflexive); antisymmetry is not part of the definition but follows from the strict partial-order axioms (exercise indicated). Exercises ask to relate reflexive closures of strict orders to ordinary partial/total orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric closure (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The symmetric closure of R is the smallest S ⊆ A×A such that R ⊆ S and S is symmetric; i.e., (1) R ⊆ S, (2) S is symmetric, (3) for every T ⊆ A×A with R ⊆ T and T symmetric, S ⊆ T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: add precisely those ordered pairs required to make R symmetric (for each (x,y) in R add (y,x) if missing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitive closure (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitive closure of R is the smallest S ⊆ A×A such that R ⊆ S and S is transitive; i.e., (1) R ⊆ S, (2) S is transitive, (3) for every T ⊆ A×A with R ⊆ T and T transitive, S ⊆ T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: close R under composition: whenever (x,y) and (y,z) are in the relation, include (x,z), iterating as necessary (possibly infinitely).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and construction of symmetric closure (Theorem 4.5.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every relation R on A has a symmetric closure; in fact S = R ∪ R^{-1} is the symmetric closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: show R ⊆ S, prove S is symmetric by case analysis on membership in R or R^{-1}, and show minimality by letting T be an arbitrary symmetric superset and proving S ⊆ T. Commentary suggests an alternative proof via taking the intersection ∩F of the family F = {T | R ⊆ T and T symmetric}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of transitive closure via intersection (Theorem 4.5.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every relation R on A has a transitive closure. Let F = {T ⊆ A×A | R ⊆ T and T is transitive}; F is nonempty (A×A ∈ F), and S = ∩F is the transitive closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: show R ⊆ S by checking each (x,y)∈R lies in every T∈F; show S is transitive by using that each T∈F is transitive; show minimality via S = ∩F ⊆ any transitive superset T. The text notes an alternative 'constructive' method (adding forced pairs repeatedly) requires induction and is deferred to a later chapter. Graph and bus-route examples illustrate intuition: transitive closure = reachability.

rubrics_metrics.name: General closure principle (smallest superset with property)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a property P (reflexive, symmetric, transitive), the P-closure of R is the smallest relation S containing R that satisfies P — equivalently the smallest element (w.r.t. ⊆) of the family F = {T ⊆ A×A | R ⊆ T and T has property P}. If F ≠ ∅ then S = ∩F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two complementary construction viewpoints: (a) form S by explicitly adjoining the minimal necessary ordered pairs (e.g., R ∪ i_A or R ∪ R^{-1}); (b) form S as intersection of all P-supersets. The book illustrates both approaches and comments on when each is convenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph / example guidance for closures
rubrics_metrics.description: Use directed graphs to visualize closures: symmetric closure turns single arrows into two-way arrows; transitive closure corresponds to reachability in the directed graph (e.g., bus-route example: include (x,y) if you can get from x to y via possibly many hops).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show how adding forced pairs propagates (in transitive closure you may be forced to add many pairs). Visualization and examples aid proof-construction and intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetric and antisymmetric relation facts (exercise 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: R is asymmetric if ∀x∀y ((x,y)∈R → (y,x)∉R). (a) If R is asymmetric then R is antisymmetric. (b) If R is a strict partial order then R is asymmetric (hence antisymmetric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are structural facts about relations; exercises ask students to prove them and to observe implications between different definitions of 'strict' and 'non-strict' order relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between strict orders and their reflexive closures (exercise / claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reflexive closure of a strict partial order is a partial order; the reflexive closure of a strict total order is a total order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are asked to prove these statements (exercise 4). This documents how to pass between 'strict' and 'non-strict' formulations of orders via reflexive closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence relation (definition 4.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: R is an equivalence relation on A iff R is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: identity relation, congruence of triangles, 'same birthday' relation, and the relation x−y∈Z on R. Equivalence relations partition the set into equivalence classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence class and quotient set (definition 4.6.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given equivalence relation R on A and x∈A, the equivalence class [x]_R = {y∈A | y R x}. The set of all equivalence classes A/R = {[x]_R | x∈A}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence classes group elements that are related; the book illustrates with concrete numeric examples and the birthday partition. Every element belongs to exactly one equivalence class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition (definition 4.6.2) and connection to equivalence classes
rubrics_metrics.description: A family F ⊆ P(A) is a partition of A if (1) ∪F = A, (2) F is pairwise disjoint (distinct elements of F are disjoint), and (3) no element of F is empty. Theorem: for an equivalence relation R on A, A/R is a partition of A (Theorem 4.6.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use basic lemmas about equivalence classes (Lemma 4.6.5): (1) x∈[x], (2) y∈[x] iff [y]=[x]. The text gives the standard proof that equivalence classes form a partition: union covers A, classes are nonempty, and distinct classes are disjoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma on equivalence-class behavior (Lemma 4.6.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an equivalence relation R on A: (1) ∀x∈A, x ∈ [x]. (2) ∀x,y∈A, y ∈ [x] iff [y] = [x].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs proceed directly from reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity. These lemmas are used to prove that equivalence classes partition A.
